steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Before every move: two questions. This part covers Question two: what is loose?; Test your own move. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Second question: which of my own pieces is **loose**, attacked and not defended? A loose piece is the easiest thing for an opponent to win. In the next board the bishop on e4 is loose. Step through it and see Black's mistake.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white knight attacks the bishop on e4, and nothing defends the bishop.

line.say: Black plays a pawn move and does not notice the loose bishop.
The knight takes the bishop for free.

claims.statement: The bishop on e4 is the only loose black piece.
If Black passes, the knight wins the bishop.

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight on f3 attacks the pawn on e5, but the knight on c6 defends it.

line.say: Black adds a second defender and opens the bishop's diagonal. The pawn on e5 is now safe twice over.

steps.text: A useful picture: every piece of yours has a number of attackers and a number of defenders. In this course, loose means attacked and undefended. Many players use the word for any undefended piece, attacked or not. If the attacker is worth less than the target, even a defended piece can be in trouble. Now find the loose piece in a new position.

Before you play a move, imagine it already made and ask what your opponent can now take. Three leaks: **1.** the moved piece lands on an attacked square. **2.** the moved piece was guarding something. **3.** the move ignores a threat already there. The next boards show the first two.

steps.caption: Black to move, thinking of the knight to b4. The pawn on a3 attacks that square.

line.say: The knight lands on a square the pawn attacks.
The pawn takes the knight. Black has lost a piece for a pawn at most.

steps.caption: Same position. Now the knight retreats to b8. Is anything left behind? It loses the e5 pawn and more (engine: about -2.5 at depth 16).

line.say: The knight steps back and no longer defends the pawn on e5.
The white knight takes the pawn, which now has no defender.

claims.statement: Before the move, one black piece defends e5.
After the move, nothing defends e5.
The retreat loses the e5 pawn and more.

steps.caption: Same position. A third idea: the bishop to b4, hoping to pin the knight on c3.

line.say: The bishop lands on b4, again a square the a3 pawn attacks.
The pawn takes the bishop. A pin means nothing if the pinning piece is lost.

steps.text: Often there is nothing to fix. Nimzowitsch, in My System, argued against the idea that every move must threaten or parry; quiet moves that improve a piece have value too. [H] Beginners may over-worry after every move. The two questions are quick: once the answer is no, follow your plan.

steps.caption: Black to move. No piece is loose and nothing White can play wins material by force; Ng5 is an idea to watch, since it would aim a second piece at f7.

line.say: The bishop develops to a good diagonal, eyeing f2. Nothing is left attacked.

claims.statement: This developing move is close to the engine's best.
